Old cells washed away

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....a new way to eliminate ageing

Unique Selling Point:
New medical breakthrough in anit-ageing treatments

Summary:
Researchers say clearing these aging cells from the body can slow down or reverse diseases such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. In a recent trial, a new drug began clearing out “zombie cells” in 30 minutes. A new study shows that removing “zombie” cells — also known as senescent (aging or deteriorating) cells — from the body has the potential to slow down or even reverse some major diseases associated with aging.

Further information:
OLD CELLS WASHED AWAY

Drug That Removes ‘Zombie’ Cells Could Help You Live Longer

Researchers say clearing these aging cells from the body can slow down or reverse diseases such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. In a recent trial, a new drug began clearing out “zombie cells” in 30 minutes. A new study shows that removing “zombie” cells — also known as senescent (aging or deteriorating) cells — from the body has the potential to slow down or even reverse some major diseases associated with aging. Scientists have long known that an accumulation of senescent cells is linked to conditions such as arthritis, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.Despite the potential shown in this recent research, Dr. James Kirkland, a professor of physiology and medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota and senior study author, emphasized that the process isn’t a magic bullet. “It’s a very preliminary study and we should plan other trials,” Dr. Kirkland told Healthline. “The biggest risk factor for most people is still their chronological age.” Think of “zombie” cells as little vacuum cleaners that no longer work efficiently. But because they still work a bit, they’re not cleared out by the body. At the same time, they’re too damaged to carry out their normal functions or repair tissue. So they clog up the works, leading to a gradual deterioration of the body. In previous studies done with animals, removing these cells reversed the aging process and extended life span. The most recent study showed improvements in humans for the first time. The three-week trial with 14 volunteers — all elderly and with pulmonary fibrosis — was intended to investigate the safety of a new drug. The fact that the test subjects were able to walk more quickly, get up from a chair more easily, and scored better in ability tests was an unintended benefit. Specifically, the results showed that after the trial, participants could walk an extra 25 yards during a 6-minute jaunt, and get up from their chairs 2 seconds more quickly. They also scored an extra point on functionality tests, moving from an average of 10 points to 11 points. “This is a glimmer that the drug might actually work. The results were impressive. All 14 people got better in their functional ability,” Kirkland told The Telegraph in England. The new treatment, named DQ, uses a drug called dasatnib, which is already licensed for killing cancer cells in people with leukemia, and the drug quercetin, a common plant pigment found in red wine, onions, green tea, apples, berries, Ginkgo biloba, and St John’s wort. The drug combination began clearing out the “zombie” cells within 30 minutes, and within 24 hours, all senescent cells were gone, the researchers reported. Pulmonary fibrosis is a scarring of the lungs that prevents oxygen moving around the body. It leads to shortness of breath, aching muscles and joints, and severe fatigue. People diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis usually survive only six to eight years after diagnosis. Researchers see the treatment potential here. “The new drug has a hit-and-run effect,” Kirkland said. “It starts working quickly, so it would be ideal to be able to give it just once a month.” The process is much like developing antibiotics, he said. Other scientists also see the potential. “We’ve known for some time that senescent cells accumulate with age and contribute directly to the aging process,” Lorna Harries, PhD, associate professor in molecular genetics at the University of Exeter in England, told Healthline. “However, until now we’ve only been able to assess the effects of drugs that target these cells in culture or animal models.” “We now suspect that many of the diseases of aging share common mechanisms,” she said, “so drugs that target senescent cells or modify their characteristics may represent a new avenue of treatment for other diseases of aging in the future.” “We still have a ways to go before this eventual aim can be realized, but this work represents an important first step,” Dr. Harries said.At this point, scientists are focusing on serious conditions where the risk-benefit analysis is in the person’s favor, Kirkland said. “There will be issues we’ll come across,” he said. “What are the side effects? What’s the right dosage? How frequently do we administer it? Will this lead to treatment for other conditions and eventually to prevention?” Dr. Francis Collins, director of the National Institutes of Health, expressed optimism but also caution in a recent blog. “Caution is warranted as we learn more about the associated risks and benefits, but it’s safe to say we’ll be hearing a lot more about senolytics in the years ahead,” Dr. Collins wrote.

Script:


V/O:
These two men are brothers…. they are actually more than brothers….they are identical twins…. The only difference between the two of them is that the one on the right has been taking a special cocktail of medicine twice a month and the other one not.
LINK:
That was just a simulation, but do not for one minute think it is far fetched at all. This could some day soon be reality. Researchers in the USA has already achieved this very same, unbelievable results in animals.
V/O:
The two mice you see here are in fact real twins. The one on the left seems frail, sickly and old, which it is. The other mouse, his identical twin, and just as old, seems vibrant and in excellent health. The only difference is the special cocktail of medicine he has been receiving for about a month now.
LINK:
What you see here is but one example of cutting-edge research in the field of anti-aging medicine, a medical discipline that is taking the world by storm.
V/O:
Dr Graige Golding is a physician and the highest qualified ant-aging specialist in Africa. He says age is a major factor health.
Craige:
When you get older your risk for diseases goes up. 90% of chronic diseases are age related. That is why people get more arthritis and diabetes and cancer and dementia and autoimmune disease and osteoporosis and so on, and so on.
V/O:
At the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota in the United States, Dr James Kirkland is one of the foremost antiaging researchers in the world. He says age related diseases have a tendency to cluster.
Kirkland:
That is when a person gets one age related disorder they tend to get another one shortly after and another one shortly after that. You find that elderly individuals are either really quite healthy or they have five or ten different conditions and be on 10 or 20 different drugs.
V/O:
And each drug is aimed at one specific organ’s problems. Up to now this has been the way modern medicine tackled disease. And it leaves much to be desired.
Graige:
Traditional or modern medicine in breaking because the body does not function as independent organ systems. The body should be considered as all one system and the different components of that system are different organ systems.
V/O:
This has led researhcers to investigate factors that are common to all age-related diseases.
Kirkland:
We find that basic aging mechanisms are operative at sites where age related chronic diseases occur.
V/O:
A number of these fundamental aging processes have been identified, and one of them that is quite prominent, is the presence of senescent or old cells.

Cells in the human body are programmed to die a natural death after some time. It is called apoptosis. But a limited number of cells simply refuse to die – they become senescent and stick around in the body.
Kirkland:
And what some of these senescent cells do, they start producing factors that damage cells around them. So they can kill cells around them, they can cause inflammation by bringing in cells from the immune system, they can destroy tissue around them, they can spread senescence to other cells, so they can become almost infectious.
LINK:
And researhcers have found that these cells, sometimes also called zombie cells, play a major role in age-related diseases.
Kirkland:
In people with diabetes we find these cells in the fat tissue, in people with Alzheimer's we find them in the brain near the lesions that cause the Alzheimer’s; around lesions in blood vessels that cause heart attacks.
V/O:
Further research established that there was a clear link between these old cells and age-related diseases. Kirkland and his team wondered what would happen if one could get rid of these old cells. They started to experiment with drugs and natural products to induce cell death in these old or zombie cells. They finally designed a cocktail that seemed to do the trick.
Kirkland:
We applied those agents in cell culture to cultured senescent cells in vitro versus non-senescent cells. Thye left the non-senescent cells alone and they resulted in the death of the senescent cells in a matter of eighteen hours or so.
V/O:
So, only senescent cells were affected and no healthy cells. Then in an animal study, they gave the medication to a litter of old mice with remarkable results. The health of the frail, old mice improved radically.
Kirkland:
So we found for example that we were able to not only delay but partially reverse age related osteoporosis; we found that we were able to alleviate diabetes and some of its complications; we were able to improve cardiac function and get new and better heart cells forming we were able to improve brain function.
V/O:
And the appearance of the mice that were give the compound was much different from their brothers and sisters. They looked younger, had more energy. They were also physically stronger – here the one that was given the medication can hold on much longer than his brother.

Not only did the removal of the old or senescent cells halt the aging process in the mice, it also seems to actually reverse it.
Kirkland:
And we are finding throughout different tissues that what we are getting is even new tissues forming that are more youthful. We found that in the case (and others) in the case of the brain we get new nerve cells forming in certian part of the brain if we clear senescent cells in conditions where nerve cell formation is impaired.
LINK:
The medication they use is a combination of an already existing cancer drug and natural plant pigments. And the medication is only given intermittently – only once every few weeks.
Kirkland:
We don’t have to have the drug continuously present in the way that you would with a drug for high blood pressure for example where it has to be constantly around. We can use what we call a hit-and-run approach much more like giving antibiotics for example.
V/O:
Because all the compounds that they are using have already been approved by the FDA in the US, they have already started with clinical trials on humans at the Mayo Clinic. The results so far are very promising and has shown that their approach to target the underlying aging process rather than single diseases, is working.
Kirkland:
It makes a lot more sense to go after age related conditions as a group instead of one at a time.
V/O:
And they discovered another benefit of the treatment – the treated mice far outlive their peers. So, it seems that removing the old cells also extends lifespan. Dr Golding does not find this surprising at all.
Graige:
You hear things like the first person who is going to live to 200 is already born. Well, this is true, we believe. Because of anti-aging medicine.
LINK:
However, longevity is not the main aim of anti-aging medicine. It is rather to prevent the onset of age-related diseases to ensue quality of life in old age.
Golding:
If people are going to be living to 80, 90 plus, which they are, then we are very focused in keeping at least three things in tact: memory, mobility and vision. Who wants to be 90 of you can’t see and walk and have no memory?
V/O:
And the strategy of removing senescent or zombie cells could see older people living quality lives, disease free, for much longer. And it could make what is still is science fiction today, a reality very soon.

The most recent study showed improvements in humans for the first time. The three-week trial with 14 volunteers — all elderly and with pulmonary fibrosis — was intended to investigate the safety of a new drug. The fact that the test subjects were able to walk more quickly, get up from a chair more easily, and scored better in ability tests was an unintended benefit. Specifically, the results showed that after the trial, participants could walk an extra 25 yards during a 6-minute jaunt, and get up from their chairs 2 seconds more quickly. They also scored an extra point on functionality tests, moving from an average of 10 points to 11 points. “This is a glimmer that the drug might actually work. The results were impressive. All 14 people got better in their functional ability,” Kirkland told The Telegraph in England. The new treatment, named DQ, uses a drug called dasatnib, which is already licensed for killing cancer cells in people with leukemia, and the drug quercetin, a common plant pigment found in red wine, onions, green tea, apples, berries, Ginkgo biloba, and St John’s wort. The drug combination began clearing out the “zombie” cells within 30 minutes, and within 24 hours, all senescent cells were gone, the researchers reported. Pulmonary fibrosis is a scarring of the lungs that prevents oxygen moving around the body. It leads to shortness of breath, aching muscles and joints, and severe fatigue. People diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis usually survive only six to eight years after diagnosis. Researchers see the treatment potential here. “The new drug has a hit-and-run effect,” Kirkland said. “It starts working quickly, so it would be ideal to be able to give it just once a month.” The process is much like developing antibiotics, he said. Other scientists also see the potential. “We’ve known for some time that senescent cells accumulate with age and contribute directly to the aging process,” Lorna Harries, PhD, associate professor in molecular genetics at the University of Exeter in England, told Healthline. “However, until now we’ve only been able to assess the effects of drugs that target these cells in culture or animal models.” “We now suspect that many of the diseases of aging share common mechanisms,” she said, “so drugs that target senescent cells or modify their characteristics may represent a new avenue of treatment for other diseases of aging in the future.” “We still have a ways to go before this eventual aim can be realized, but this work represents an important first step,” Dr. Harries said.At this point, scientists are focusing on serious conditions where the risk-benefit analysis is in the person’s favor, Kirkland said. “There will be issues we’ll come across,” he said. “What are the side effects? What’s the right dosage? How frequently do we administer it? Will this lead to treatment for other conditions and eventually to prevention?” Dr. Francis Collins, director of the National Institutes of Health, expressed optimism but also caution in a recent blog. “Caution is warranted as we learn more about the associated risks and benefits, but it’s safe to say we’ll be hearing a lot more about senolytics in the years ahead,” Dr. Collins wrote. Interviewees: USA -- Dr Kirkland, leader of the study at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota South Africa -- Dr Craige Golding, a specialist physician in anti-aging medicine. he is also South Africa's highest qualified ant-ageing specialist
